The classic signs are face drooping, arm weakness, and speech difficulty on one side. Warning signs can come on suddenly, including a severe headache, face drooping, or one-sided weakness. Call 911 right away if they are happening now.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Common early signs of type 2 diabetes include frequent urination, excessive thirst, constant hunger, fatigue, blurred vision, and slow-healing sores. Many people also notice dry skin or skin that itches more than usual. Type 2 diabetes is usually linked to weight, family history, and activity level. If you have risk factors and new symptoms, book a visit with your care team.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Common side effects of ibuprofen are upset stomach, dizziness, and mild headache. More serious ones include bleeding in the stomach, black tarry stools, and swelling of the legs. People with stomach problems or on blood thinners should talk to their doctor before taking it.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
For adults 65 and older, the CDC recommends the shingles vaccine (Shingrix), the pneumonia vaccine (Pneumovax), and the flu shot every year. Your care team can tell you which ones apply to you.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Pneumonia is usually diagnosed with a chest X-ray, but a fast-acting blood test can tell if there's a bacterial infection. Your care team will decide whether to start antibiotics right away based on the test results.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
A healthy diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol, regular exercise, and not smoking all help lower LDL ("bad") cholesterol. Ask your care team about a lipid panel and whether a cholesterol-lowering plan is right for you.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Floaters are small specks or shadows in your vision that drift as you move your eyes. They're common with age as the vitreous gel inside the eye changes and breaks apart. Most floaters are harmless, but a sudden increase, flashes of light, or a shadow over your vision can mean a retinal tear, which needs immediate eye care.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Tension-type headaches are usually mild, feel like a tight band around the head, and don't come with fever, weakness, or vision changes. Migraines are often one-sided, throbbing, and may be accompanied by nausea, sensitivity to light, or auras. Keeping a headache diary can help you tell them apart.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Most people can wait until their next routine visit for a skin check, but any mole that grows, changes color, itches, or bleeds should be looked at right away. If you have many moles or a family history of skin cancer, you should be checked more often.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
A heart attack often starts with chest pressure or squeezing, like a heavy weight or tight band, and can spread to the arm, jaw, or back. It may come with pain, sweating, nausea, or shortness of breath. Some people, especially women and older adults, have fewer classic symptoms. If someone has these symptoms now, call 911 even though they aren't getting worse - emergency care can prevent lasting damage.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
Most adults should start regular screening at age 50, but people with risk factors like a family history or inflammatory bowel disease may need to start earlier. Your care team can tell you what screening is right for you based on your age, family history, and medical history.

<triage>{"level": "ROUTINE", "red_flags": [], "concern": "general health question"}</triage>
A cold is usually milder than the flu and often starts gradually, with symptoms like a runny nose, congestion, and a mild cough. Flu symptoms tend to come on suddenly and include high fever, body aches, fatigue, and sometimes a dry cough. People with risk factors should be tested if they have these symptoms.
